sm: John Stossel argues that the biggest things in life happen without a central planner, and that government plans, from job-creation promises to Soviet economic formulas, tend to fail. He uses a skating rink as an example of spontaneous order: people avoid collisions on their own, and when he and a former Olympic skater tried giving instructions, skaters did worse. He also points to schools of fish, flocks of birds, the evolution of English, and the unused invented language Esperanto. The Soviet Union produced long lines, empty shelves and the poor East German Trabant car, which vanished once competition arrived. He says American medicine is heavily planned because most dollars are paid by third parties, while LASIK eye surgery, paid for by patients, has seen innovation, short waits and falling prices. He concludes that a few rules are still needed, such as don't hit people, don't take their stuff, and keep your promises.
